prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Croton has wilting leaves after repotting

I have repotted my Croton 10 days ago after noticing, that the soil it was in wasn’t really absorbing any water and bottom leaves drying out and dropping every week or so.

It was doing fine, but I noticed yesterday, that leaves started to wilt and I am unsure what to do.

The soil I used this time is 1:1:1 potting soil (fertilized), leca and pine barks.

What I noticed is, that the soil is quite wet (s. Last photo, watering indicator is fully blue) even though I watered last when I repotted the plant (10 days ago).

No, it was in the soil i bought it in before, which clearly wasn’t taking in any water and the plant was losing a bottom leave every 1-2 weeks.

I have humidifiers at home, humidity is about 50% usually

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
**Most likely: root damage from the old wet soil, now made worse by transplant shock and a soil mix that stays wet.** Wilting while the soil is still soaked usually means the roots can't draw water. Dead and dying roots lose the ability to absorb water, so a plant wilts from thirst even though the soil is wet. Your meter reading fully blue ten days after watering fits that. Repotting also injures fine roots, and the root system then struggles to keep up with the leaves' water demands, causing temporary wilting.

**Other possibilities:**
- **Poor drainage at the base.** The terracotta pot sits inside a decorative lilac basket. If water collects there, the roots sit in it. Check whether the basket holds water.
- **Transplant shock alone.** This is possible if the roots are white and firm when you check them. Your stem base looks firm in the photo, which is encouraging.

**Quick check that decides it:** Lift the plant out and look at the roots. Healthy roots are firm and white, while rotting roots are mushy and brown. Also smell the root ball. A sour or swampy odor points to rot.

**Fix:**
1. **Stop watering now.** Don't add water to a wilting plant with soggy soil.
2. **Unpot and trim.** Use sterile scissors or pruning shears to trim away every rotted root you can see. If the roots are healthy, leave them alone and just remove the loose, wet soil.
3. **Repot into a drainage pot.** Remove the decorative basket or make sure water can't pool in it. Use a chunkier mix with more bark and leca and less dense potting soil. Your current mix may be holding too much water.
4. **Water only when the top inch or so is dry.** Allow the surface of the rootball to feel almost dry before watering. Keep the plant in bright light, away from drafts. Your 50% humidity is fine.

Expect some more leaf drop while the roots recover. New growth is the sign that it's working.
